sample_size.excerpt: A case-control study, performed in two towns of Serbia (Yugoslavia) from 1990 to 1994, comprised 101 patients with histologically confirmed prostate cancer and 202 hospital controls individually matched by age (+/-2 years), hospital admittance and place of residence.
sample_size.location: Abstract, sentence 1; total_n derived from reported group counts 101 + 202 = 303

cases.excerpt: A case-control study, performed in two towns of Serbia (Yugoslavia) from 1990 to 1994, comprised 101 patients with histologically confirmed prostate cancer and 202 hospital controls individually matched by age (+/-2 years), hospital admittance and place of residence.

effect_size.excerpt: After adjustment for possible confounders, risk factors for prostate cancer appeared to be the highest tertile of protein (odds ratio (OR) = 13.54, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 2.38-77.13), saturated fatty acid (OR = 3.63, 95% CI = 1.03-12.79), fibre (OR = 4.02, 95% CI = 1.38-11.73), and vitamin B12 intake (OR = 2.07, 95% CI = 1.08-3.97); a protective effect was found for the highest tertile of alpha-tocopherol (OR = 0.15, 95% CI = 0.05-0.53), calcium (OR = 0.37, 95% CI = 0.14-0.99) and iron intake (OR = 0.34, 95% CI = 0.12-0.95).

headline.funnel_interpretation: The significant funnel plot asymmetry (egger's p=0.0067) indicates substantial publication bias in this meta-analysis on calcium and prostate cancer. This specific pattern suggests that smaller studies with smaller or null effects may be underrepresented, compromising the reliability of the pooled estimate and potentially leading to an overestimation of the true association.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 28 studies yielded an overall effect size of 1.18 (95% CI: 1.1–1.28), suggesting that calcium is associated with a higher risk of prostate cancer. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was very high between-study heterogeneity (I² = 80.69%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.
